A user writes in: "I add a task and nothing happens. Then I type in the search box and my task suddenly shows up." The code looks innocent: it pushes the new task into the
. The setter is right there, so React should know. It doesn't, and the task appearing later, at a random moment, is the clue to why.
The belief: the setter is the signal. Change the data however you like,
, then call the setter and React re-renders with the new data.

It's a natural belief if you've used other tools. Many reactive UI libraries track mutations by wrapping your objects in proxies, and plenty of backend code updates objects in place. In React it even half works: mutate, and the next render that happens for any other reason will show your change, which is exactly why the task above appears after typing. That accidental success is what makes the bug so confusing.
The setter compares references, not contents
. If they're identical, React skips re-rendering the component and its children. For arrays and objects, identical means the same reference.
changes what's inside the array, but it's still the same array, so
hands React the value it already has. No render. The new task sits in memory until something else, like typing in the search box, re-renders the list, and the render reads the mutated array.

Why doesn't React just look inside? A deep comparison on every update would cost time in proportion to the size of your data, and watching objects for edits would mean wrapping them in proxies. React does neither: it never touches your objects. That's why you can keep any object in state, however large, at no extra cost, as long as you replace it instead of editing it.

The array you pushed into is also the one the previous render used. React's docs call each render's state a snapshot; mutating it changes that snapshot after the fact. Logs you printed earlier now show the new contents, and any code that compares old and new values sees "no change". That includes
dependency checks. The docs spell out the bargain: if you never mutate,

is enough to know nothing inside changed. That one fast check powers React's optimizations, and features like undo, a change history or resetting a form get much easier when old values are never overwritten.
The fix is to treat state as
: never change it, replace it. Build a new array or object that differs where you need it, and pass that to the setter:
